content:
Quran 4:156 condemns some of the Jews for "their saying against Mary a great slander" (buhtān 'aẓīm). In 19:27-28 her people say to her: "Your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste."[1] A critic asks for evidence that anyone made such a charge. Without it, the verse looks like an accusation invented by its author.

The written record answers the question. The charge that Jesus was born of adultery is attested more than four centuries before Islam. This article aims to provide context to that charge, insha'Allah, in six answers that give the sources with their dates and say where the dating is uncertain.

The Greek philosopher Celsus wrote a book against the Christians in about 178. Origen, answering him seventy years later, quotes the "Jew" whom Celsus brings on stage. This speaker says that Mary was convicted of adultery with a soldier named Panthera, and that her husband put her out.[2]

In De spectaculis 30, written in about 197, Tertullian imagines the mockers of Jesus calling him the son of a carpenter and of a woman who sold herself.[3]

The charge was current in North Africa within twenty years of Celsus.

Tosefta Hullin 2:22-23 mentions healing "in the name of Yeshu ben Pantera". The passage names him and does not itself say that he was born of adultery.[4]

The Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 104b; Sanhedrin 67a) explains the name "Ben Stada" as the son of a Miriam who strayed from her husband, with Pandera as her lover. Peter Schäfer dates this material in the Bavli to the late Sasanian period, close to the time of the Quran or a little before it.[4]

Sanhedrin 43a, often quoted in this debate, concerns the execution of Jesus and says nothing about his birth.[4]

The Toledot Yeshu, a Jewish counter-gospel, survives in many versions. Some may draw on late antique material, and Agobard of Lyon knew a form of it in the ninth century. The fullest versions of the Pandera story are medieval.[5]

It shows the charge living on in Jewish polemic, as the Quran says it did.

The Quran ascribes the slander to a group (4:156), and it puts Mary's chastity at the centre of her story (19:20; 21:91; 66:12). It defends her in the words her own people are made to use (19:27-28).[1]

The record shows the charge from the second century to the sixth. The verse answers a charge that was in circulation.

The Babylonian Talmud was taking its final shape in the same centuries as the Quran's revelation, and its account of Pandera is the charge in written form. The Quran answered a slander that was current among the people it addressed.[4]

The Quran defends Mary against a charge that is attested centuries before it. Our related articles are 6 prophets both books share and Talmud, midrash and apocrypha: borrowing claims. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 4:156, 19:20, 19:27-28, 21:91, 66:12.
  2. Origen, Contra Celsum 1.28 and 1.32, trans. Henry Chadwick (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1953).
  3. Tertullian, De spectaculis 30.
  4. Tosefta Hullin 2:22-23; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 104b, Sanhedrin 67a and 43a; Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2007), chapter 1.
  5. Peter Schäfer, Michael Meerson and Yaacov Deutsch (eds.), Toledot Yeshu ("The Life Story of Jesus") Revisited (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2011); Michael Meerson and Peter Schäfer, Toledot Yeshu: The Life Story of Jesus, 2 vols. (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2014).
